# Measure a region with a defined boundary

[Time actual local work, accumulate laps and reduce a maximum without confusing it with an end-to-end benchmark.]{.lesson-deck}
:::

A timer is useful only when its boundaries are clear. This refactors the
old sleeping FFT placeholder into three actual distributed cosine sums.
The environment initializes MPI before the timer calls `MPI_Wtime`.

## Time the local work, then communicate

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="laps" dedent=2}
```

Each rank owns cyclic sample indices. The numerical checksum has the
independent exact value $\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\cos(2\pi j/N)=0$, for $N=4096$.
The reduction is outside the timed region. `duration()` accumulates the
three completed laps on each rank; the final reductions report the maximum
and mean of those accumulated durations.

The maximum local work duration is not the elapsed time of the whole run:
it excludes the reductions, startup and output. The code makes no speedup
claim. It also does not compare unsynchronised absolute clock readings
between ranks; each elapsed interval is formed on its own rank.

## Check arithmetic without asserting a speed

```sh
openpfc run model.cpp input.json --launcher=none
openpfc run model.cpp input.json --ranks=2 --launcher=mpirun
```

The empty input is unused. The CSV reports rank count, lap count, checksum,
maximum duration and mean duration. The checks require finite nonnegative
durations, maximum at least mean, and the cosine-sum identity. They do not
assert that a particular machine finishes in a fixed number of microseconds.

Change `n`, then move the reduction inside the timing boundary and explain
what the new quantity includes. Call `reset()` before a fresh measurement
series; every `toc()` must have a matching `tic()`. Continue with
[structured profiling](../profiling/index.qmd), which gives names and
nesting to regions across accepted frames. The
[timer header](https://github.com/VTT-ProperTune/OpenPFC/blob/master/include/openpfc/kernel/mpi/timer.hpp)
defines lap accumulation.

The complete [C++ model](model.cpp) and [starting input](input.json)
are available with this lesson.
